visit_body.visit1:
Early ANC care
• Start antenatal care early (before 12 weeks if possible).
• Attend all scheduled ANC visits for you and your baby’s health.

ANC visits
• Go for regular check-ups to monitor your health and your baby’s growth.
• Keep your ANC card and follow health worker advice.

Danger signs
• Seek medical care immediately for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, severe headache, fever, swelling, reduced baby movement, or difficulty breathing.
visit_body.visit2:
Iron and folic acid
• Take daily iron-folic acid (IFA) tablets as advised by your health worker.
• IFA helps prevent anaemia and supports your baby’s growth.

Calcium supplementation
• Take calcium tablets as recommended during pregnancy.
• Calcium helps keep your bones and your baby’s bones healthy.

Pre-eclampsia monitoring
• Monitor for swelling and high blood pressure (pre-eclampsia).
visit_body.visit3:
Birth preparedness
• Plan where you will give birth and how you will reach the facility.
• Save emergency contacts and keep necessary items ready.

Skilled birth care
• Giving birth with a skilled health worker helps keep mother and baby safe.
• Go to a health facility when labour starts.

Mental wellbeing
• Feeling worried or tired can happen during pregnancy.
• Talk to someone you trust if you feel stressed, sad, or overwhelmed.
visit_body.visit4:
Preparing for baby care
• Learn about breastfeeding, newborn care, and danger signs before delivery.
• Plan support from family after birth.

Avoid harmful substances
• Avoid alcohol, tobacco, and other harmful substances during pregnancy.
• Avoid taking medicines without advice from a health worker.

Hygiene and infection prevention
• Wash hands regularly and use safe drinking water.
• Keep food clean and well cooked.

anc.nutrition_body:
Healthy diet
• Eat a balanced diet using affordable local foods (rice, dal, vegetables, eggs, fish, fruits).
• Eat small, frequent meals if you feel nauseous.

prep.visit1: Bring your antenatal card or previous medical reports. Note the date of your last period, and any questions you want to ask your health worker.
prep.visit2: Bring your antenatal card. Note any headaches, blurred vision, or swelling in your hands or face to discuss with your health worker.
prep.visit3: Bring your antenatal card. Discuss your birth plan, emergency transport, and family support for delivery.
prep.visit4: Bring your antenatal card. Review danger signs of labour, pack clean baby clothes, and confirm hospital emergency numbers.

physical_activity.point2: Rest when tired and stop if you feel pain, dizziness, breathing problems, or bleeding.

pre_eclampsia_monitoring.point1: Know the warning signs. High blood pressure during pregnancy can be dangerous. Have your blood pressure checked at your ANC visits.
pre_eclampsia_monitoring.point2: Some swelling of the feet can happen during pregnancy. Sudden or severe swelling of your face or hands can be a warning sign.
pre_eclampsia_monitoring.point3:
Get medical help quickly if you have:
• a very bad headache
• blurred vision or seeing spots
• severe pain in your upper belly
• sudden swelling of your face or hands
• trouble breathing
• feeling very unwell
pre_eclampsia_monitoring.point4: Do not wait for your next ANC visit if you have these signs.

signs_of_labour.point1: Regular stomach tightening or pain that comes and goes and becomes stronger over time.
signs_of_labour.point3: A small amount of blood-mixed mucus coming out from the vagina ("show").
signs_of_labour.point4: Water leaking from the vagina (the baby's water breaking).
signs_of_labour.point5: Feeling more pressure in the lower abdomen or feeling that the baby is moving down.

labour_go_to_facility.point1: Labour pain starts and becomes regular or stronger.
labour_go_to_facility.point2: Water breaks or fluid starts leaking from the vagina.
labour_go_to_facility.point3: There is any bleeding from the vagina.
labour_go_to_facility.point4: Labour pain continues for more than 12 hours without delivery.
labour_go_to_facility.point7: You have severe headache or blurred vision.
labour_go_to_facility.point9: You feel very weak, dizzy, or have difficulty breathing.
labour_go_to_facility.point10: Your hands, feet, or face become suddenly swollen.
labour_go_to_facility.point11: Your baby's movements decrease or stop.
labour_go_to_facility.point12: A healthcare provider advises you to come to the facility.

contact_body.contact1:
Rest
• Rest as much as you can. Ask family to help with chores.

Bleeding
• Some bleeding is normal. Heavy bleeding is not. Please go to the health facility.
contact_body.contact2:
Pain
• Mild pain is normal. Severe pain is not normal.

Eating
• Eat extra food and drink extra water every day.
contact_body.contact3:
Cleanliness
• Wash your hands and body area with clean water daily.

Check-up
• See a health worker at day 3–4, day 7–14, and week 6.
contact_body.contact4:
Family planning
• Ask your health worker about spacing your next pregnancy.

Mood
• Feeling sad or worried after birth is common. If it continues or gets worse, please speak to a health professional.

pnc.breastfeeding_body:
Start early
• Start breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth.

Only breastmilk
• Give only breastmilk. No water, honey, or other food for 6 months.

Feed often
• Feed your baby whenever they want, day and night.

Good position
• Hold baby close, tummy to tummy, mouth open wide on the breast.

Enough milk
• Baby feeding well: wet nappies, good weight gain, calm after feeding.

Sore breasts
• Painful or swollen breasts? See a health worker soon.

Both breasts
• Offer both breasts at each feed.

Get help
• If feeding is hard, ask a health worker; don't stop on your own.

prep.contact1: Keep baby warm with skin-to-skin contact. Inform your health worker of any heavy bleeding, fever, or difficulty feeding.
prep.contact2: Ensure baby is breastfeeding well on demand. Keep the umbilical cord dry and check for any redness or discharge.
prep.contact3: Bring your and baby's health cards. Discuss your healing, postpartum rest, and baby's growth.
prep.contact4: Bring your health records. Discuss family planning options, routine vaccines, and your emotional wellbeing.

cord_healing.point1: Your baby's umbilical cord needs time to dry and heal after birth.
cord_healing.point2: Keep the cord clean and dry.
cord_healing.point3: Wash your hands with soap and clean water before touching the cord or your baby.
cord_healing.point4: Keep the cord outside the diaper so it stays clean and dry.
cord_healing.point5: Let the cord dry and fall off naturally. Do not pull it off, even when it is almost detached.
cord_healing.point6: Do not put oil, powder, ash, turmeric, or other substances on the cord unless advised by a health professional.
cord_healing.point7: A small amount of drying or a little blood when the cord separates can happen.
cord_healing.point8: Keep checking the cord while it heals.
cord_healing.point9: If the area becomes very red or swollen, has pus or a bad smell, or your baby develops a fever or becomes very unwell, seek medical help promptly.
cord_healing.point10: With simple clean and dry care, your baby's cord can heal safely.

pnc.routine_care_blurb: Simple daily care to keep your baby warm, fed, clean, and safe.

keep_baby_warm.point1: Keep your baby close to you.
keep_baby_warm.point2: Use skin-to-skin contact to keep your baby warm.
keep_baby_warm.point3: Dress your baby appropriately for the weather.
keep_baby_warm.point4: Keep your baby away from cold air and smoke.

routine_breastfeed.point1: Start breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth.
routine_breastfeed.point2: Give only breastmilk for the first 6 months.
routine_breastfeed.point3: Breastfeed whenever your baby is hungry, during the day and night.
routine_breastfeed.point4: Do not give water, honey or other foods during the first 6 months.

keep_baby_clean.point1: Wash your hands before touching or feeding your baby.
keep_baby_clean.point2: Keep the umbilical cord clean and dry.
keep_baby_clean.point3: Do not put anything on the baby's umbilical cord unless advised by a health worker.
keep_baby_clean.point4: Keep your baby's clothes and sleeping area clean.

keep_baby_safe.point1: Always place your baby on their back to sleep.
keep_baby_safe.point2: Keep the baby's sleeping area free from pillows, blankets and other objects that may cover the baby's face.
keep_baby_safe.point3: Keep your baby away from smoke and harmful substances.

baby_checkups.point1: Take your baby for newborn check-ups as advised.
baby_checkups.point3: Ask your health worker if you have concerns about feeding, growth or development.

vaccines_after_birth.point1: Vaccines help protect your newborn from serious diseases.
vaccines_after_birth.point2: Ask your health worker which vaccines your baby should receive soon after birth.
vaccines_after_birth.point3: Take your baby for the recommended birth vaccines before leaving the health facility, when advised.
vaccines_after_birth.point4: Keep your baby's vaccination card safe. It helps you remember which vaccines your baby has received and which are due next.
vaccines_after_birth.point5: Do not worry if your baby receives more than one vaccine at a visit. Each vaccine helps protect your baby from different diseases.
vaccines_after_birth.point6: Giving your baby vaccines on time is a simple and important way to protect their health.

childhood_immunisation.point1: Your baby needs vaccines from birth and throughout childhood.
childhood_immunisation.point2: Vaccines protect children from serious diseases and help them grow up healthy.
childhood_immunisation.point3: Follow the vaccination schedule given by your health worker or vaccination centre.
childhood_immunisation.point4: Try not to miss any vaccine date. Put the next vaccination date in your phone or calendar as a reminder.
childhood_immunisation.point5: Keep the vaccination card safe and take it with you whenever your child receives a vaccine.
childhood_immunisation.point6: If your child misses a vaccine, do not give up. Talk to your health worker about when your child can receive the missed dose.
childhood_immunisation.point7: Your child may have mild soreness, swelling, or fever after some vaccines. These reactions are usually short-lived; ask your health worker what to do if you are concerned.
childhood_immunisation.point8: Even if your child looks healthy, vaccines are still important because they help prevent diseases before your child is exposed to them.
childhood_immunisation.point9: Every vaccine is another step towards a healthier childhood. Keep your child's vaccines up to date.

tt.about_body:
What tetanus is, and how it affects mothers and newborns
• Tetanus is caused by a germ that can get into the body through a dirty cut or wound, even the cut made when a baby's cord is cut. It makes the body go very stiff and can kill if not treated fast in hospital.

Why newborns are especially at risk of tetanus
• A newborn baby can get tetanus through the cord cut at birth. This can happen if the cord is cut with a dirty blade, or if things like ash, oil, mud, or cow dung are put on the cord instead of keeping it clean and dry.
• Warning: If your baby cannot suck, becomes stiff, or has fits in the first month of life, please go to the hospital right away. This is an emergency.

How TT vaccination protects both the mother and the baby
• The TT vaccine helps your body fight tetanus. When you get this vaccine during pregnancy, some of this protection passes to your baby before birth. This keeps your baby safe from tetanus in the first weeks of life. The vaccine is safe for you and your baby.

Why Bangladesh uses a 5-dose lifetime schedule
• You need up to 5 TT doses in your whole life, not every pregnancy. Each dose adds more protection. Once you have had all 5, you and your future babies are protected. You will not need this vaccine again.
• Note: How many tetanus vaccinations you need can be different for each woman. Your health worker will check your card and tell you which shot you need today. Just follow what your health worker tells you. You don't need to count the doses yourself.

If you have already had some TT doses before (previous pregnancy or as a teenager)
• If you had TT doses before in an earlier pregnancy, at school, or at another clinic, that is good. The app will not guess this for you. Please tell your health worker and show your card if you have it. They will tell you exactly which dose you need next.

Maternal immunisation
• Take recommended vaccines during pregnancy to protect you and your baby.
• Follow the schedule advised by your health worker.
tt.epi_card_body:
Bring your EPI (Expanded Programme on Immunization) immunisation card
• Please bring your EPI card to every ANC visit. Your health worker needs to see it to know how many doses you already had, and which dose you need next. If you cannot find your card, tell your health worker. They will help you.
